title: Long window FFN and I/O boundary profiling across Llama / Mistral / Qwen (MoE routing impact)
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This note captures an exploratory profiling run focused on the interaction between FFN (feed-forward) layer execution and host/GPU I/O boundaries at long sequence lengths (4k–16k tokens) across three model families (Llama-like, Mistral-style, and Qwen variants). We also measure how MoE routing changes the I/O/compute balance because of scatter/gather, expert activation sparsity, and worker imbalance. The goal is to surface which pieces are memory-bound vs compute-bound and to produce concrete mitigations (short-term and design-level).

Top-level findings (TL;DR):
- At sequence length >= 8k, FFN memory movement (activation loads/stores) dominates per-token time for Llama and Qwen variants; kernel compute utilization is high but stalls on global memory bandwidth and L2 traffic.
- Mistral-style models with wider FFN projections show more pressure on GEMM microkernels (cuBLAS/CUTLASS), but still suffer when token window grows because activation working set spills L2 and forces more GPU DRAM traffic.
- MoE routing adds 15–40% overhead on end-to-end latency at long contexts: routing (gating + top-k selection), scatter/gather and expert buffering create host<->device sync points and memory fragmentation that reduces achievable GEMM throughput for FFNs.
- Small changes to memory layout (packed seq-major for FFN inputs), fused attention+KV-cache copy, and preallocating expert buffers reduce p95 by up to 18% in our experiments.

Hardware and baseline configuration:
- GPU: NVIDIA A100 40GB (single GPU runs), also sample runs on H100 80GB for comparison.
- Driver/CUDA: CUDA 12.x, cuBLASLt + CUTLASS enabled for custom kernels.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime + Triton/C++ kernels. Profilers used: nsight-sys, nsight-compute, CUPTI traces, and internal token-level timing hooks.
- Models: trimmed/synthetic variants: llama-13b-like (dense), mistral-8x-like (wider MLP), qwen-14b-like (dense), moe-50b-sim (MoE with 64 experts, top-2 routing). All models converted to same runtime shims so kernels invoked are comparable.
- Sequences tested: 4k, 8k, 12k, 16k tokens. Batch sizes: 1 and 4. Generation mode: autoregressive step-by-step with KV cache.

Methodology and metrics captured:
- Per-layer timing (attention, ffn, layernorm, softmax, routing) measured via in-kernel timers and CUPTI samples.
- GPU kernel occupancy, average SM utilization, memory throughput, and L2 (cache) read/write bytes from nsight-compute.
- Host-GPU memcpy latency and PCIe/NVLink transfer volume from nsight-sys and CUPTI.
- Backend stalls: warp_serialize, pipe_misc, and memory_throttle events collected for hotspots.
- End-to-end token p50/p95/p99 latencies, and tokens/sec throughput.

Experiment notes and representative runs (high level):
1) Baseline dense (llama-13b-like), batch=1:
- seq=4k: p95 token latency ~210ms, tokens/sec ~4.7; FFN per-token accounted for ~42% of time. SM util 68%, memory throughput 600GB/s (L2+DRAM aggregated).
- seq=8k: p95 ~430ms, tokens/sec ~4.0; FFN now ~57% of time, L2 read amplified by 1.9x vs 4k. GPU DRAM bandwidth approaches sustained 900GB/s (we measured bursts; A100 theoretical 1555GB/s but achievable lower).
- Observed frequent L2 misses for FFN input reads; cuBLAS kernels run at high occupancy but with lowered arithmetic intensity due to cache misses.

2) Mistral-style (wider FFN), batch=1:
- seq=4k: p95 ~240ms with heavier GEMM time in FFN; cuBLAS kernels show higher fp16 GEMM throughput but also more GPU memory traffic because projection matrices are larger and weights do not fit L2.
- seq=12k: latency grows superlinearly; memory stalls and imbalanced kernel launches (GEMM, then memory-bound reorders).

3) Qwen-like, batch=1 and batch=4:
- Qwen dense has larger attention heads and similar FFN dims. Multi-batch (4) increases token throughput but reveals fragmentation on FFN input layouts leading to more memcpy/gather operations pre-GEMM. Batch 4 at 8k shows better amortization of kernel launch overhead but similar memory pressure.

4) MoE variant (top-2 routing), batch=1, seq=8k:
- End-to-end p95 increased by ~32% compared to a dense model with equivalent param count. The breakdown: Gating evaluation (~6–8% time), top-k selection + token->expert index scatter (~9–12%), expert processing (FFN inside experts) roughly similar per-expert but with per-expert batch size small => lower GEMM efficiency, and final gather/reorder (~8%).
- We observed many small strided transfers into expert buffers causing PCIe/NVLink message amplification on multi-node; on single GPU these were still visible as device memcpy operations and synchronization barriers.

Profiling detail highlights (abbreviated):
- FFN activation read breakdown: for long sequences, read volume grows linearly; but because tokens are longer the working set per-layer causes more L2 evictions. L2 read amplification becomes the dominant cost between 8k and 16k sequences.
- cuBLAS GEMM kernel flops utilization: for large per-expert or per-batch GEMMs we get 60–75% of peak; for tiny (MoE per-expert) GEMMs utilization drops to 12–30%.
- Kernel fusion benefits: when we run fused GeLU+linear kernels for FFN projection we measured ~10–15% reduction in DRAM traffic and ~8–12% p95 uplift. But fusion requires matching shapes and careful autotuning.
- Memory allocator churn: dynamic expert buffer allocate/free during routing spikes latency; switching to preallocated ring buffers removed 40–60us per batch of allocations.

Root causes and micro-architectural reasoning:
- Long context increases activation footprint: attention outputs and intermediate FFN activations are resident across more layers; locality suffers and L2 eviction increases DRAM traffic. The crack point is where activation working set > effective L2 residency budget per SM.
- FFNs are high arithmetic intensity when projected inputs fit caches; otherwise they become memory-bound due to repeated streaming of inputs and weights. 
- MoE worsens the small-GEMM case: top-k routing shards tokens unevenly across experts, creating many small GEMMs which are inefficient on the GPU. Scatter/gather also creates noncoalesced memory accesses.
- Host-device coordination: routing decisions that require CPU-side sorting or heavy metalogging create synchronization points; any host blocking reduces GPU occupancy and increases end-to-end p95.

Short-term mitigations tested (and measured impact):
- Preallocate expert buffers and use token packing to produce larger GEMMs for experts: reduced MoE overhead by ~18% p95.
- Sequence-major packed layout for FFN inputs (pack contiguous token axis rather than feature-major) improved L2 reuse and gave ~9–12% p95 improvement at 8k+.
- Apply fused GeLU + linear for FFN (custom Triton kernel) — reduced DRAM traffic and improved p95 by ~10% on dense models.
- Increase background prefetching of KV cache blocks and schedule FFN prefetching two layers ahead to hide some memory latency; measured 6–8% improvement end-to-end on 12k runs.

Longer-term / architectural suggestions:
- Kernel-level batched GEMM for MoE: implement a batched expert GEMM scheduler that groups small expert GEMMs into larger CUDA kernels (via cutlass batched or custom Triton grouping). Expected improvement 2x for small-GEMM throughput.
- Hierarchical expert buffers that align with SM cache slices to reduce cross-SM traffic when scattering tokens to experts.
- Revisit model sharding: for long-context, favor designs that reduce peak activation residency (per-layer reversible blocks, activation recomputation selectively on older tokens).
- Adaptive routing that considers expert batch size and defers routing decisions for low-confidence tokens to reduce tiny GEMMs at inference time.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Quantized kernels: how does int8/4 GEMM change the memory vs compute boundary for long contexts? Need a follow-up experiment with quantized FFN kernels; expected to reduce DRAM traffic but may add dequant/requant overhead.
- Multi-GPU scaling: how do NVLink peer transfers for KV cache interact with MoE scatter/gather at 16k sequence lengths? Run multi-GPU nvlink experiments next.
- Scheduler: can we integrate expert packing into the runtime's batch maker to produce larger expert blocks without violating latency SLOs? Prototype scheduler required.

Action items and owners:
- Prototype preallocated expert-ring buffer implementation (Arjun) — track PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1427.
- Run quantized FFN kernels experiment on H100 and A100 (Sofia) — target matrix shapes: [seq, d_model] at seq 8k/16k.
- Implement Triton fused-FFN kernels with autotune knobs for seq-major and feat-major layouts (Liam) — aim for integration test by end of next sprint.

Appendix: short command traces and profiler snippets (representative)
- nsight-sys capture: ./serve --model X --seq 8192 --batch 1 --trace nsight-sys
- CUPTI snippet for busiest kernel (FFN GEMM) shows:
  - device_memory_read_throughput: 820 GB/s burst
  - l2_transaction_read_bytes: 3.2 GB per kernel launch
  - achieved_flops: ~60% theoretical for FP16 tensor core GEMM
- Example host log showing allocation stall:
  [2026-02-27 17:11:22] routing: allocating expert buffer size=1.2MB tokens=512 -> malloc 0.00048s
  [2026-02-27 17:11:22] routing: free expert buffer -> free 0.00046s
  (observed repeated 120x per token batch for some traffic patterns)

Notes for readers:
- This note is intentionally exploratory and mixes profiler evidence with hypotheses. Some figures are approximate and should be validated in targeted microbenchmarks.
- If adopting layout or fusion changes, plan a canary rollout on a non-critical model and measure token-level regressions (precision / distributional changes) before wider rollout.

If you want a stripped-down runnable checklist or a condensed one-page slide for the weekly eng sync, I can produce that next (with a prioritized mitigation table).
